content: Synchronized ventilation is a standard practice for neonatal care in industrialized countries. Two primary modes of synchronized ventilation, flow-cycled and time-cycled, are commonly used to provide respiratory support to neonates. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of flow-cycled versus time-cycled synchronized ventilation on the risk of developing bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) at 36 weeks postmenstrual age in neonates requiring assisted ventilation. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) in The Cochrane Library (Issue 4, 2009), PubMed (from January 1966 to October 2009), EMBASE (from January 1974 to October 2009), and CINAHL (from January 1982 to October 2009). References and cross-references from identified studies were also reviewed. Additionally, abstracts from the Pediatric Academic Societies Meetings (from January 1990 to October 2009) were manually searched. No language restrictions were applied during the search process. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomized or quasi-randomized clinical trials that compared flow-cycled and time-cycled synchronized endotracheal ventilation in neonates. These studies needed to report at least one relevant outcome to be considered. Literature searches were conducted by one author, while study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two authors. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion among all authors. Ultimately, only two small, short-term, randomized, individual cross-over trials met the inclusion criteria. These trials involved a total of 19 preterm neonates. Both studies focused on lung mechanics and short-term respiratory physiology outcomes but did not provide data on clinical morbidities or mortality. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to determine the safety and efficacy of flow-cycled compared to time-cycled synchronized ventilation in neonates. They emphasized the need for large, randomized clinical trials with a parallel-group design that report on clinically significant outcomes to address this gap in evidence.
